An elevated transferrin saturation greater than or equal to 45% (per the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases and the American College of Gastroenterology) is highly suspicious for hereditary hemochromatosis (HHC) and requires genotyping, which may confirm the diagnosis of HFE-associated HHC. C
The mainstay of therapy is regularly scheduled phlebotomy with interval checking to be sure the serum ferritin level remains below 50 mcg/L. C
Cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, arthropathy, and diabetes are complications of untreated hemochromatosis. B

background.definition: Hereditary hemochromatosis (HHC) is a disorder that causes progressive expansion of the plasma iron pool and includes at least 4 types of genetic iron overload conditions involving gene mutations related to iron metabolism. summarizes the spectrum of HHC as a subset of iron-overload syndromes.

list.listitem: The estimated prevalence of HFE mutations in the Unites States is 5.4% for the C282Y gene and 13.5% for the H63D gene (estimated 0.26% homozygosity for C282Y and 1.89% homozygosity for H63D).

It is estimated that 4.4 per 1000 white adults in North America are homozygous (C282Y/C282Y) for this mutation. Those at the highest risk for disease onset are white men between the ages of 30 years and 50 years who have northern European ancestry.
Clinical penetrance varies. In one large community screening program, only 1 in 152 persons homozygous for C282Y was found to have multiorgan disease.
Inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, the most prevalent mutation involves a tyrosine substitution for a cysteine at amino acid 282 (C282Y) of the HFE gene.
Most individuals with HHC have the homozygous mutation C282Y, but may also have H63D (compound heterozygosity).
Environmental and lifestyle factors potentially affect the phenotypic expression, which appears to vary widely among individuals.
Because of mutant gene(s), feedback mechanisms normally responsible for controlling iron absorption/storage are disrupted affecting key iron-regulatory proteins, including hepcidin and ferroportin.
The tissue iron burden increases as ferroportin-mediated iron export goes unchecked due to loss of or resistance to hepcidin, a central iron-regulatory protein.
Parenchymal cell iron deposition leads to organ damage, especially liver damage. Iron-mediated damage can also occur in the heart, joints, pancreas, brain, and skin.
The true risk for clinical disease has not been defined even among those who are C282Y homozygotes because biochemical penetrance does not equate to clinical penetrance of the disease.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Homozygosity or heterozygosity of the C282Y gene
White men of northern European descent, between the ages of 30 years and 50 years
Relatively high levels of serum ascorbic acid

list.listitem: Despite higher risks of diabetes or liver disease among C282Y homozygotes, screening for hereditary HFE-associated hemochromatosis in the general population is not recommended because of a relatively low clinical penetrance of the disease. The American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases, American College of Gastroenterology, and European Association for the Study of the Liver all recommend against routine genetic screening for HHC in asymptomatic general population. B
The American College of Physicians also found insufficient evidence to recommend, for or against, the use of transferrin saturation and serum ferritin levels to identify early stages of HHC.C

The American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases, the American College of Gastroenterology, and the European Association for the Study of the Liver all recommend testing to determine genotype for individuals with serologic evidence of elevated ferritin or transferrin, as well as adult first-degree relatives of those confirmed C282Y/C282Y homozygotes. C
Patients may be asymptomatic, or present with nonspecific symptoms, elevated hepatic transaminases, chronic liver disease, or diabetes. C

Serum transferrin saturation greater than or equal to 45% and increased ferritin (>300 mcg/L in men or >200 mcg/L in premenopausal women) suggest HHC and warrant further investigation, including genotyping.C
Homozygosity for the C282Y mutation or combined heterozygosity (C282Y/H63D) genotype in the HFE gene analysis confirms HFE associated HHC diagnosis. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Impaired erythropoiesis; low hepcidin can cause increased iron absorption from GI tract
Heinz bodies present on staining peripheral smear with crystal violet; Hb electrophoresis abnormal; poor use of iron in erythropoiesis
RBCs are destroyed; decreased haptoglobin, and increased reticulocyte count, LDH, unconjugated bilirubin; iron gets released
Antimitochondrial antibodies present in 90% to 95% of cases; liver disease lowers hepcidin

Differential.Differential_Name: Chronic liver disease (alcohol, nonalcohol, viral hepatitis)
Differential.Differential_Features: Liver disease lowers hepcidin; HC typically has hepatic iron values of 200-800 mcmol/g dry wt (normal <35) and hepatic iron index >2 in homozygotes
History of multiple transfusions for refractory anemias/myelodysplastic syndrome variants (up to 100 units PRBC)
Deficient activity of heme synthetic enzyme uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase; photosensitivity causes scarring, irregular pigmentation, and hair growth
Inappropriately low transferrin saturation and reduced tolerance to phlebotomy; autosomal recessive disorder
Signs and symptoms of neurologic disease; iron buids up due to decreased expression of the frataxin gene
Gestational alloimmune liver disease of fetus; rare

list.listitem: Many patients are asymptomatic. In a 1997 series, 78% of patients had normal physical examination results and 73% were asymptomatic. Cirrhosis (3%) and diabetes (2%) were uncommon at presentation.
Signs and symptoms are often nonspecific (eg, arthralgias, impotence, severe fatigue or subtle neurocognitive changes) and may be mistaken for other maladies.
Ask about a family history or personal history of iron-overload conditions, fatty liver disease, cirrhosis, elevated liver function tests, or diabetes in patients suspected of HHC.

Right upper quadrant pain, jaundice/icterus, spider angiomas, and hepatomegaly may be present because of iron deposition in liver. Skin hyperpigmentation with or without hemosiderin stains may be seen. Joint pain in hands and/or feet or poor grip strength due to arthropathy or arthritis may be discovered on examination. The European Alliance of Associations for Rheumatology developed 2025 Classification Criteria for Hemochromatosis Arthropathy in C282Y homozygotes, but it needs further external validation.
Lower extremity edema and arrhythmia may be present as signs of iron deposition in cardiac tissue. Endocrine involvement may manifest as testicular atrophy and gynecomastia in men.
In a series of 93 Canadian homozygous patients diagnosed with HHC, abdominal pain was seen in 16%, joint pain in 11%, and weakness in 9%; 38% of male patients reported loss of libido and impotence.

If hemochromatosis is clinically suspected, order serum transferrin saturation and ferritin (see ). Serum transferrin saturation is calculated as the ratio of serum iron to total iron-binding capacity. Elevated serum transferrin saturation of 45% or higher, or elevated ferritin (>200 mcg/L in premenopausal women, >300 mcg/L in others) warrants HFE gene testing. Fasting labs are not required, though can be helpful with borderline results.
Genotype testing that reveals homozygosity for the C282Y mutation or the heterozygote C282Y/H63D genotype in the HFE gene analysis confirms the diagnosis of HHC.
The American College of Gastroenterology recommends seeking a secondary cause for those with iron overload who are not C282Y homozygotes.

Once the HFE HHC diagnosis is confirmed, serum ferritin and liver function tests help determine therapy (see ). A serum ferritin level greater than 1000 mcg/L is predictive of advanced fibrosis in patients with HHC (50 of 89 with elevated ferritin, only 1 of 92 without).
Unsaturated iron-binding capacity has been shown to be a worthwhile test to use with or without transferrin saturation in detecting iron-overload disorders including HFE-associated HHC.

Hepatic iron concentration and/or hepatic iron index have been used to aid in diagnosis. Hepatic iron index greater than 1.9 can accurately differentiate between homozygous and heterozygous HHC, alcoholism, and normal population.

Liver biopsy is generally used for diagnosis in the presence of comorbidities and for prognosis and management when serum ferritin is greater than 1000 μg/L. Hepatic MRI imaging provides a noninvasive, semiquantitative approach to measure liver iron concentration and may be useful to avoid liver biopsy.
Severe iron overload may be calculated from the number of phlebotomies required to deplete iron stores.
See diagnostic algorithm in .
Hemochromatosis may be categorized as HFE-associated or non-HFE-associated ().

Hemochromatosis classification was updated by the BIOIRON Society to include: HFE-related (C282Y homozygosity or compound heterozygosity with other HFE pathogenic variants), non-HFE-related (HJV, HAMP, TFR2, SLC40A1), digenic (C282Y heterozygosity with non-HFE gene, or other combination of non-HFE genes), and molecularly undefined types (molecular characterization still unknown).
Non-HFE hemochromatosis (see Differential Diagnosis table) is still important to evaluate, as it is also associated with liver fibrosis and liver disease.
Phlebotomy is the first line and mainstay of treatment for HHC. C
There is insufficient evidence for the efficacy and safety of erythrocytapheresis (isolated removal of red cells instead of whole blood) over phlebotomy. C
Dietary modification has minimal impact on iron overload.C
If phlebotomy is not tolerated or is contraindicated, chelation therapy may be an option. C

Chelation can be used second line when blood loss from phlebotomy is poorly tolerated or contraindicated, as with more profound anemia or hypoproteinemia. Deferoxamine given parenterally removes approximately 10 to 20 mg iron per day.

Subcutaneous deferoxamine, oral deferipone and oral deferasirox are chelators that are approved by the FDA for other secondary iron overload conditions and used off-label for hereditary hemochromatosis.
Adjunct proton pump inhibitor use for a year was found to reduce the number of phlebotomies needed for maintenance therapy.
BBI-001 is being evaluated as an oral iron-binding medication that may be effective, especially for hyper-absorbers of dietary iron, as a safer alternative to chelators.
A hepcidin mimetic (rusfertide) has been shown to prevent iron re-accumulation and lower transferrin saturation after undergoing iron-lowering phlebotomy treatment, though it is not yet FDA-approved.

Phlebotomy is the first-line and mainstay of treatment for HHC. While it has not been evaluated in randomized controlled trials, studies comparing phlebotomy to placebo or no treatment are unlikely to be conducted given the ethical implications.

Phlebotomy appears safe and effective in decreasing body iron stores. It is performed once or twice weekly with 500 mL of blood removed per session (200 to 250 mg iron). Treatment effect is monitored using serum ferritin.

Weekly sessions removing 500 mL blood for 1 to 2 years may be necessary because as much as 25 g or more of iron may have to be removed. Maintenance phlebotomies are required generally every 3 months to keep serum ferritin levels less than 50 μg/L.
There is insufficient evidence for the efficacy and safety of erythrocytapheresis (isolated removal of red cells instead of whole blood) over phlebotomy.
Liver transplant for HHC patients with liver failure has been shown to have good short- and long-term outcomes, when compared to liver transplant for other reasons.
A normal lifespan is expected if the disorder is caught early, prior to cirrhosis or diabetes. C
Cirrhosis is associated with a heightened risk of hepatocellular carcinoma and mortality.B
The standardized incidence ratio for hepatocellular carcinoma in HHC homozygotes is 21 (95% CI, 16-22). The absolute risk of liver cancer is 6% in men and 1.5% in women over a 10-year period.B
The natural history of HHC is poorly understood because of variable biochemical/genetic factors resulting in a spectrum of clinically expressed phenotypes.

Persons with hereditary hemochromatosis and concomitant hepatic steatosis, viral hepatitis, or heavy alcohol use are at an increased risk of developing liver injury due to the synergic effect of inflammatory hepatic pathology and iron overload.

Poor outcomes due to liver failure/cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma can occur; it is important to assess for liver fibrosis after diagnosing HHC. Ferritin >1000 mcg/L, elevated aminotransferases, and low platelets can predict cirrhosis in >80% of patients.
A restrictive or infiltrative cardiomyopathy can cause significant morbidity and mortality in those with C282Y homozygosity who are left untreated.
Diabetes can occur from iron penetration with direct cytotoxic effects to pancreatic beta cells.
A large meta-analysis did not show any statistically significant association between C282Y homozygotes and components of metabolic syndrome.
Overall mortality is somewhat higher in patients with a transferrin saturation greater than 55% (RR = 1.6; 95% CI, 1.1-2.5).

Life expectancy is improved by the removal of excessive body iron burden, with a 5-year survival rate between 33% and 89%, and diabetes improves after serum ferritin level declines to less than 50 μg/L.
Symptoms of arthropathy and hypogonadism do not appear to improve significantly with the removal of excess iron.
If patients are treated early enough in the course of the disease, hepatic damage, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma may be averted.

In a prospective cohort study of 1847 Swedish patients with hereditary hemochromatosis, the standardized incidence ratio for hepatocellular carcinoma was 21 (95% CI, 16-22). There was no significant increase in the risk of nonhepatocellular cancers. After 10 years, the absolute risk of liver cancer was 6% in men and 1.5% in women.
A second study confirmed this relative risk.
This risk is seen in patients with HHC-related cirrhosis.
Serum ferritin needs to be periodically monitored during treatment.
Serum ferritin may be checked at each phlebotomy visit (3-4 months), but some experts suggest annual measurement.
The optimal interval for measuring serum ferritin has not been described and depends on the patient's genetic predisposition and environmental factors.

Transferrin saturation levels are not currently included in management guidelines for HHC, though some researchers correlate them with fatigue and joint pain, calling for studies comparing ferritin only versus ferritin plus transferrin saturation-guided treatment of HHC.
Pregnant women with hemochromatosis and mild-moderate iron overload can pause their phlebotomy treatments during pregnancy.
Neonatal hemochromatosis is exceedingly rare.

cell.label: Hemochromatosis (HC) suspected based on laboratory test results (eg, ferritin, serum iron, ALT, AST), family history of HC, or symptoms of HC. Order transferrin saturation.*
Order serum ferritin and hepatic transaminases (ALT, AST).
Repeat transferring saturation in 3 months, and consider other diagnoses.
Reassure. Consider retest later if symptoms persist. Consider other diagnoses.

footnotes.footnote: *Transferrin saturation = (serum iron concentration/total iron-binding capacity) x 100.
†Confirmation of these genotypes confirms the diagnosis of HFE hereditary hemochromatosis.
